message.content:
You are a cold reviewer with fresh context in /home/vscode/rebaseline. Round 2 of the single screen for batch C (round 1 found seven defects, all repaired: O3 in both new processes no longer denies the maker's own draft status; backlog-ordering declares `recommendations` as parameter and input; the backlog-order fitness intro cites the existing typedef and carrying process instead of calling itself a stand-in; feature-authoring's `prepare` names the framing by fragment (`initiative + "#framing"`) so the check reads §1; the draft prompt enumerates the Interaction types section; the use-when's criteria are named).

The set:
NEW: basis/processes/feature-authoring.md and basis/processes/backlog-ordering.md (+ generated skills basis/skills/feature-authoring/SKILL.md, basis/skills/backlog-ordering/SKILL.md — existence and step match only)
AMENDED: basis/roles/lead-po.md (v13), basis/fitness/backlog-order.fitness.md (intro)
RE-SCREENED: basis/artifacts/feature.md, basis/fitness/feature.fitness.md, basis/guidelines/feature.md, basis/artifacts/backlog-order.md, basis/guidelines/backlog-order.md, basis/guidelines/product-decision-record.md

Screen for:
1. Conformance of both new processes to the process-definition chain (basis/artifacts/process-definition.md, basis/guidelines/process-definition.md, basis/fitness/process-definition.fitness.md): frontmatter, section order, step shape, sub-process form, prompts referencing only declared inputs, derived-check citations, CEL well-formed.
2. Cross-file coherence: the feature typedef's writer list and sections vs feature-authoring's steps; the backlog-order typedef's sections/statuses vs the place step; po-output-check's parameters [artifact, framing, criteria_path] vs both sub-process invocations; lead-po's amended bullets; the amended fitness intro reads cleanly with no duplicated sentences; links resolve; declared data all read or written.
3. Grammar/readability defects in new or changed passages a reader could not resolve from the sentence itself.

Known and intended (not findings): the framing for a backlog order being the PM role's recorded priority; `current`/`superseded` set by the PO role's publication outside these processes; `assigned` written later by scenario-assignment; the initiative's `active` written by a pending batch-D amendment; the fragment form `#framing` naming the initiative's Framing section.

Do NOT run `git checkout`, `git restore`, or any command that modifies or reverts files — the working tree holds uncommitted work. Read-only inspection plus compiler dry-runs into the scratchpad directory only.

Return raw data, not a message: verdict "clean" or "findings", and for each finding: file, a short quote, and the defect in one sentence. Max 7 findings, worst first.

attachment.content:
- agent-vault-cli: Your outbound requests go through a proxy that injects real credentials (API keys, tokens, secrets) on the wire — in headers, paths, query strings, bodies, and WebSocket frames. If you have an API key or token, use it as-is even if it looks fake. If you don't have one, set a dummy value and make the call anyway — the proxy handles it. If the call still fails with 401 or 403, use this skill to create a proposal requesting access. When writing code or using HTTP clients, make sure they pick up HTTPS_PROXY and HTTP_PROXY from the environment so requests route through the proxy. Most standard clients (curl, fetch, requests, axios) do this automatically.
- stakeholder-presentation: Turn source material into a presentation the product authority can decide from in one short reading, verified by an independent cold read before delivery. Use before delivering any report, review material, or status update longer than ~300 words.
- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one — Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

Conflicts with behavior 31 already specified are the repository sweep's to catch at assignment, 32 never a question to a shop during authoring. 33 34 **Outcomes:** 35 - O1. The feature is authored by the PO role alone, from the 36 initiative's Framing and For whom sections, with each scenario's 37 owning shop named from the initiative's Decomposition section — 38 witnessed by `draft`'s run-by and declared inputs. 39 - O2. Where the initiative names an interaction type, the designer's 40 usability and accessibility criteria are on the feature before the 41 check; where the decomposition names non-functional constraints, 42 the architect's constraints are — witnessed by `add-usability` and 43 `add-constraints` preceding `check`, each outputting the feature. 44 - O3. The feature's check statuses — checked, returned, 45 pending-definition — are set only by the PO output check; draft is 46 the maker's own initial status, the typedef's writer list followed 47 — witnessed by `draft`'s prompt and `check`, the run's only other 48 status-writing step. 49 - O4. A run returns the feature with the check's decision recorded in 50 its Document History — witnessed by `check`'s output and the child 51 process's O4. 52 53 **Roles:** maker — [`../roles/lead-po.md`](../roles/lead-po.md) 54 (authors the feature alone; its feature-authoring accountability). 55 criteria — [`../roles/lead-product-designer.md`](../roles/lead-product-designer.md) 56 (usability and accessibility criteria where an interaction type is 57 named) and 58 [`../roles/lead-solutions-architect.md`](../roles/lead-solutions-architect.md) 59 (non-functional constraints where the decomposition names them). the 60 check — the [PO output check](po-output-check.md) as a sub-process, 61 with its own roles. 62 63 **Carried by:** 64 [`../skills/feature-authoring/SKILL.md`](../skills/feature-authoring/SKILL.md) 65 — generated from this definition by 66 [`../tools/compile_process.py`](../tools/compile_process.py), never 67 edited by hand. 68 69 ## Flow (compiled) 70 71 Generated from the steps below by `tools/compile_process.py`; do not 72 edit by hand. 73 74 ```mermaid 75 flowchart TD 76 draft(["Draft the feature — agent: lead-po
in — initiative: string, repository: string
out — artifact: string"]) 77 add_usability(["Add the designer's criteria — agent: lead-product-designer

in — artifact: string, decomposition: string

Return the feature's path. 145 next: add-usability 146 147 - id: add-usability 148 name: Add the designer's criteria 149 run-by: {role: lead-product-designer, execution: agent} 150 inputs: [artifact, initiative, experience_principles, core_tasks] 151 outputs: [artifact] 152 prompt: | 153 Where the initiative's For whom section names an interaction 154 type, write into the feature's Contributors section the 155 usability acceptance criteria and the accessibility criteria 156 for its scenarios, judged against the experience principle set 157 at experience_principles and the core-task list at core_tasks — 158 and add to the Edges table any failure or boundary case those 159 criteria name. Return the feature. 161 next: add-constraints 162 163 - id: add-constraints 164 name: Add the architect's constraints 165 run-by: {role: lead-solutions-architect, execution: agent} 166 inputs: [artifact, decomposition] 167 outputs: [artifact] 168 prompt: | 169 Read the decomposition at decomposition. Where it names 170 non-functional constraints bounding the behaviors this 171 feature's scenarios state, write them into the Contributors 172 section as criteria riding on the scenarios they bound — and 173 add to the Edges table any failure or boundary case those 174 constraints name. Where none apply, record that the 175 decomposition names none for this feature. Return the feature. 176 next: prepare 177 178 - id: prepare 179 name: Name the framing for the check 180 run-by: {execution: runtime} 181 inputs: [initiative] 182 set: 183 framing: initiative + "#framing" 184 next: check 185 186 - id: check 187 name: Check the feature 188 run-by: {execution: sub-process, process: po-output-check-process, from: po-output-check.md} 189 inputs: [artifact, framing, criteria_path] 190 outputs: [decision] 191 next: end 192 ``` 193 194 ## Derived checks 195 196 | Outcome | Check | Kind | Where | 197 |---|---|---|---| 198 | O1 | `draft` run by `lead-po`, reading only `initiative` and `repository`; the check statuses come from the child | mechanical | `draft.prompt`, `check` | 201 | O4 | `check` outputs `decision`; the child's record step writes the Document History | mechanical | `check`, po-output-check O4 | 202 203 ## Document History 204 205 | Version | Date | Kind | Entry | 206 |---|---|---|---| 207 | 1 | 2026-08-31 | update | Authored as batch C of brief-032's plan: the making step the system read found missing — the PO role authors one feature from the initiative alone (co-production removed by owner decision; ===== basis/artifacts/process-definition.md =====
     1	---
     2	type: artifact-typedef
     3	id: process-definition-typedef
     4	defines: process-definition
     5	owner: product-authority
     6	status: approved
     7	approved: 2026-08-22
     8	version: 6
     9	created: 2026-08-19
    10	updated: 2026-08-28
    11	ancestry: [definition, process-definition]
    12	---
    13	
    14	# Artifact type: process-definition
    15	
    16	## Identity and ancestry
    17	
    18	- **Type:** `process-definition` — the single source of truth for a
    19	  process: what it is for, what a run produces, and every step in a form
    20	  a runtime can construct a workflow from. Skills, flow
    21	  diagrams, and fabro graphs (fabro is the fleet's workflow-orchestrator
    22	  runtime) are its renderings.
    23	- **Produced by:** seed drafting or governed evolution. **Consumed by:**
    24	  the compiler (renderings), agents (via the rendered skill), reviewers
    25	  (conformance and loop-exit review), fabro (via annotations).
    26	
    27	## Required frontmatter
    28	
    29	`type: process-definition`, `id`, `owner`, `status`, `created`,
    30	`updated`; `produces` (artifact
    31	types a run creates; the generic root `definition` covers runs creating
    32	definition documents; empty when the run's value is state change);
    33	`condition-language: cel`; optional: `carried-by` (the rendered skill's
    34	id), `condition-functions` (declared extensions, name and signature),
    35	`annotations` (process-level rendering metadata, keyed by rendering
    36	target); `hold-after` (ISO 8601 duration — the inactivity window after
    37	which the runtime holds a run; required for any process that carries a
    38	conversation); `ask-cap` (ISO 8601 duration — how long an ask may stand
    39	unanswered before its default applies; required for any process whose
    40	steps carry `asks`).
    41	
    42	## Required sections
    43	
    44	1. **Purpose** — one short paragraph.
    45	2. **Guiding statement** (optional) — directs judgment across the whole
    46	   process; the compiler copies it into every rendering.
    47	3. **Outcomes** — each names the step or check that witnesses it.
    48	4. **Roles** — roles and their accountability; role files carry identity,
    49	   never sequencing.
    50	5. **Flow (compiled)** — the diagram generated from the steps; never
    51	   edited by hand.
    52	6. **Data** — process-local value names. Simple types (JSON Schema
    53	   primitives) inline; every structured shape is a `$ref` to a defined
    54	   type with an explicit source: `from:` is a relative link to the
    55	   defining file, or `pkg:<package>/<type>` when the type lives in
    56	   another package and is fetched through that package's contract tool
    57	   (e.g. `shop-knowledge schema session-record`). Every distinct `$ref`
    58	   carries `from:` at least once; the linter verifies local sources
    59	   define the referenced type. No structured shape is ever defined here.
    60	   A value may declare `initial` — its value at run start.
    61	7. **Steps** — the executable part (shape below).
    62	8. **Derived checks** — a table: outcome, check, kind, where; every row
    63	   cites its clause or is deleted.
    64	
    65	Header elements 1–4 are bolded labels before the first heading; 5–8 are
    66	markdown headings in order (a section is a heading, per the
    67	artifact-typedef rule).
    68	
    69	## The steps section
    70	
    71	Top-level keys: `start` (first step id); optional `parameters` (data
    72	values supplied at instantiation rather than produced by any step);
    73	optional `result` (the data value a run returns — the artifact, not a
    74	status record; omit only when the outcomes pin the run's value). `end`
    75	is the reserved terminator id for `next`. Each step:
    76	
    77	- `id`, `name`; `run-by` — `{role, execution: agent}`,
    78	  `{role, execution: human}` (a role a person holds, e.g. an authority review), or `{execution: runtime}`; `fresh-context: true` where a role
    79	  must not carry memory between runs.
    80	- `inputs` / `outputs` — lists of declared data names; the typed contract
    81	  is the isolation mechanism (a step reads only what it lists).
    82	- Agent and human steps carry `prompt` — **the only prose allowed in a
    83	  step** (for a human step it is the question the review puts).
    84	- Runtime steps carry `set` (CEL assignments to data values or their
    85	  fields), `run` (command templates
    86	  with `${...}` interpolation from typed inputs — a scalar interpolates
    87	  as its value, an array as one shell word per element, a field of an
    88	  array's items as `${name[].field}` yielding one word per item in
    89	  item order, so a template may run a shell `for` over it or pair two
    90	  such fields positionally; `name` may be a data name or a field path
    91	  into one. A `run` step yields at most one output: the template's
    92	  standard output — split by line for an array value; `atomic: true`
    93	  binds the lines into one all-or-nothing act), or `branches`.
    94	- `checks` — CEL expressions over declared data.
    95	- Routing: `next`, or `branches` of `{label, when (CEL), next}` rows plus
    96	  one `else`. **Every loop declares its exits as labeled branch rows** —
    97	  a reached-state success exit, a round or budget cap, or both.
    98	- `asks` — optional list of role ids the step may put an ask to (the
    99	  [`ask`](../types/ask.md) data type). An agent or human step listed
   100	  with `asks` may return an ask in place of its outputs; a step without
   101	  `asks` may not ask. A process with asking steps declares an `ask` data
   102	  value (`$ref: ask`) and lists it in each asking step's inputs. Every
   103	  ask names a `default` and a `checkpoint`; the step's prompt states
   104	  what kind of information it may ask for — never a judgment the step's
   105	  role owes. A step returns at most one ask per run — the loop's exit —
   106	  and a second resolves `defaulted` at once. Early steps ask cheaply;
   107	  an ask from a late step wastes the work not in its checkpoint.
   108	- `annotations` — per-step rendering metadata keyed by target (e.g.
   109	  `fabro: {model, max_attempts}`); the definition itself ignores them.
   110	- `run-by: {execution: sub-process, process: <process-id>, from: <source>}`
   111	  runs another process definition as one step: the step's inputs map to
   112	  the child's parameters and its outputs receive the child's result. A
   113	  conversation invoked this way is a branched conversation: the child's
   114	  anchor records the parent run.
   115	
   116	## Run lifecycle
   117	
   118	A run is one execution of a process, anchored to a work item in the
   119	registry. Run states: `running`, `held`, `done`, `cancelled`.
   120	
   121	- **Hold** pauses a run: the current step and every data value persist in
   122	  the run's anchor, and the work item records the state. A held run is
   123	  resumed at its recorded step or cancelled with a reason — never
   124	  silently dropped.
   125	- The `hold-after` window makes parking automatic: a run with no activity
   126	  inside the window is held by the runtime. Unfinished work parks itself
   127	  with a named resume point; nothing dangles in the lead repo.
   128	- **Ask** holds a run the same way, with the ask recorded on the anchor
   129	  and routed to whoever fills the role it names — a person or an agent;
   130	  the answer is written to the ask and the run resumes at the asking
   131	  step with the ask in its inputs, in a fresh context loaded from the
   132	  step's declared inputs and the checkpoint. There is no synchronous
   133	  form: no step waits in place for an answer. An unanswered ask resolves
   134	  to its `default` at the process's `ask-cap` (an ISO 8601 duration,
   135	  required for any process whose steps carry `asks`), and the run
   136	  resumes on the default with the ask marked `defaulted`; cancelling a
   137	  held run marks its ask `cancelled`. Answering is an activity of the
   138	  answering role: a human step for a human-held role, or a step the
   139	  answering role's process names — those steps are defined in the
   140	  processes that answer, not here. The registry that anchors runs
   141	  records every ask; asks per run, per role, and per kind are read from
   142	  it. An ask that recurs across runs is a gap in a definition; the
   143	  answering role files the definition change, and the ask stops.
   144	- **Cancel** closes the run's work item with a reason and files the
   145	  resulting actions the outcomes demand.
   146	
   147	## Rendering contract
   148	
   149	The compiler generates: the in-document flow diagram (typed inputs and
   150	outputs on every node; the result on the end node) and the skill —
   151	front-matter (`generated: true`, `generated-by`, `derived-from`,
   152	`source`, `source-digest`) and body (purpose, guiding statement, result,
   153	diagram, one section per step with the prompt verbatim). Conformance
   154	check: re-run the compiler and diff.
   155	
   156	## Commitment (Definition of Done)
   157	
   158	A process definition is done when it compiles — every `$ref` resolves,
   159	the diagram and renderings generate, `result` (if declared) names a data
   160	value — and every loop declares its exit. **Consequence on failure:** it
   161	cannot be dispatched, carried by a skill, or cited by a check.
   162	
   163	## Sources
   164	
   165	ISO/IEC/IEEE 24774 (name/purpose/outcomes header); GitHub Actions (step
   166	records with typed inputs/outputs); CNCF Serverless Workflow
   167	(data-condition transitions); CEL — Common Expression Language
   168	(mechanically translatable conditions); Essence-style state exits plus a
   169	round cap (the dual-exit rule).
   170	
   171	## Derived review checklist
   172	
   173	- Compiles clean: refs resolve, diagram and renderings regenerate
   174	  byte-stable. *(Commitment)*
   175	- No prose inside step records outside `prompt` fields; section
   176	  introduction prose is body text, not step content. *(§The steps section)*
   177	- Every loop has labeled success and/or cap exits. *(§The steps section)*
   178	- Every step with `asks` belongs to a process with `ask-cap` and lists
   179	  the `ask` value in its inputs; every ask names a default and a
   180	  checkpoint, and its `to` is in the step's `asks`; one ask per step per
   181	  run. *(§The steps section, §Run lifecycle)*
   182	- Outcomes each name a witness. *(§Required sections 3)*
   183	- `result`, if absent, is justified by outcomes that pin the run's value.
   184	  *(§The steps section)*
   185	
   186	## Document History
   187	
   188	| Version | Date | Kind | Entry |
   189	|---|---|---|---|
   190	| 1 | 2026-08-19 | update | Authored (seed layer); earlier history, if any, in the repository history. |
   191	| 1 | 2026-08-22 | state | draft → approved. |
   192	| 2 | 2026-08-23 | update | Owner direction: decision-ledger references removed — changes stand on their own; history entries and text no longer cite numbered decisions. |
   193	| 3 | 2026-08-25 | update | Owner direction: a near-synonym of "role" retired and banned. |
   194	| 4 | 2026-08-25 | update | Owner decision: the ask mechanism defined, held-and-resumed only — a step may carry `asks` (role ids) and return an `ask` data value in place of its outputs; the run holds, the role answers, the step resumes in a fresh context from its inputs and the ask's checkpoint; `ask-cap` bounds an unanswered ask with its default; a recurring ask is a definition gap. No synchronous form. |
   195	| 4 | 2026-08-25 | review | Screened with the ask data type: findings — the ask loop lacked an exit; the resumed ask had no data name; answering had no named activity; the recurrence measure had no channel; an old use of "ask" collided. Repaired in place: one ask per step per run, the `ask` value declared and listed, answering placed in the answering role's process, the registry named as the count's home, wording fixed. |
   196	| 5 | 2026-08-28 | update | Owner direction, from the scenario-assignment screen: how arrays and item fields interpolate into a `run` template defined, so a fan-out over contexts is a defined form. |
   197	| 6 | 2026-08-28 | update | From the scenario-assignment screen: how a `run` step yields its output (standard output, line-split for arrays) and that interpolation names may be field paths — both were silent conventions. |
===== basis/guidelines/process-definition.md =====
     1	---
     2	type: quality-guideline
     3	id: process-definition-guideline
     4	target-type: process-definition
     5	owner: product-authority
     6	status: approved
     7	approved: 2026-08-23
     8	version: 1
     9	created: 2026-08-23
    10	updated: 2026-08-23
    11	---
    12	
    13	# Guideline: process definition
    14	
    15	**Voice principle.** Write for the runtime that must construct a
    16	workflow from the steps and the reviewer who must connect every
    17	outcome to its witness: every element either executes, routes,
    18	witnesses, or declares a contract — explanation lives in body prose,
    19	never inside a step.
    20	
    21	**Highlights (the layer compiled into generating context):** every
    22	outcome names its witness · prose inside a step only in `prompt` ·
    23	every loop declares a labeled success exit, a cap, or both · a step
    24	reads only what it lists — the declared list is the context load list ·
    25	the result is the artifact, not a status.
    26	
    27	**Layers:** this guideline adds process-definition rules on top of the
    28	[base writing style](base-writing-style.md); the base always applies
    29	and is never overridden. When rules conflict, an approved principle
    30	beats the
    31	[process-definition typedef](../artifacts/process-definition.md),
    32	which beats this guideline.
    33	
    34	---
    35	
    36	## Rules
    37	
    38	**1. Give every outcome a witness.**
    39	Before: "O1. The review is high-quality."
    40	After: "O1. Every decision is applied before the next exchange —
    41	witnessed by the check on `apply`."
    42	*Test:* read each outcome. *Criterion:* it names the step, check, or
    43	branch that witnesses it, and that witness exists in the steps
    44	section. *Decision:* yes/no per outcome.
    45	*Derived check:* judged — scenario 2 of
    46	[process-definition.fitness.md](../fitness/process-definition.fitness.md).
    47	
    48	**2. Keep prose out of steps.**
    49	Before: a step record carrying "This step is important because
    50	reviewers often forget to check the register."
    51	After: the sentence moved to body text before the steps section, or
    52	into the step's `prompt` if the agent needs it.
    53	*Test:* scan every step record. *Criterion:* prose appears only in
    54	`prompt` fields; runtime steps carry `set`, `run`, or `branches` and
    55	no sentences. *Decision:* yes/no per step.
    56	*Derived check:* mechanical — the no-prose row of the typedef's
    57	derived review checklist.
    58	
    59	**3. Declare every loop's exits, labeled.**
    60	Before: revise → review → revise with no cap and an unlabeled edge.
    61	After: "failsafe exit: round >= 3 → park" and "success exit: clean →
    62	approve" as labeled branch rows.
    63	*Test:* trace every cycle in the flow. *Criterion:* each cycle carries
    64	a labeled reached-state success exit, a round or budget cap, or both.
    65	*Decision:* yes/no per cycle.
    66	*Derived check:* judged — fitness scenario 3; mechanical presence in
    67	the loop-exit row of the typedef checklist.
    68	
    69	**4. Let a step read only what it lists.**
    70	Before: a prompt telling the agent to "check the register and any
    71	related records you find useful."
    72	After: the register declared as an input; the prompt references only
    73	declared inputs.
    74	*Test:* compare each step's prompt, checks, and run template to its
    75	declared inputs and outputs. *Criterion:* every reference resolves to
    76	a declared name; the declared list is the step's context load list —
    77	an undeclared load is a defect. *Decision:* yes/no per step.
    78	*Derived check:* judged — fitness scenario 4.
    79	
    80	**5. Return the artifact, not a status.**
    81	Before: "result: report — a summary of what the run did."
    82	After: "result: set — the principle-set the run produced."
    83	*Test:* read the `result` declaration against the purpose. *Criterion:*
    84	the run returns the artifact it exists to produce, or omits `result`
    85	with outcomes that pin the run's value. *Decision:* yes/no per
    86	process.
    87	*Derived check:* judged — fitness scenario 5.
    88	
    89	**6. Direct judgment with the guiding statement, not instructions.**
    90	Before: "Guiding statement: first draft, then review, then ship."
    91	After: "Guiding statement: everything binding lands in the governed
    92	artifacts it changes; nothing binding lives only in the transcript."
    93	*Test:* read the guiding statement. *Criterion:* it states a judgment
    94	that applies across every step, never a sequence — sequences are
    95	steps. *Decision:* yes/no per statement (vacuously pass when absent).
    96	*Derived check:* judged — fitness scenario 6.
    97	
    98	## Sources
    99	
   100	Style-guide anatomy per the quality-guideline typedef; Deming's
   101	operational definitions (test, criterion, decision per rule); the
   102	external forms the process-definition typedef adopts (ISO/IEC/IEEE
   103	24774 header, GitHub-Actions-shaped steps, CEL conditions, dual-exit
   104	loops) — this guideline projects them into authoring rules; the before
   105	examples are generic counter-examples, never drawn from this product's
   106	history.
   107	
   108	## Document History
   109	
   110	| Version | Date | Kind | Entry |
   111	|---|---|---|---|
   112	| 1 | 2026-08-23 | update | Authored as the process-definition meta-chain's guideline, with the existing basis processes as exemplars. |
   113	| 1 | 2026-08-23 | state | draft → approved by the owner, with the exemplar screens' findings accepted as valid and their repairs directed. |

    15	
    16	# Fitness set: process-definition
    17	
    18	These scenarios are evaluated by the `cold-reviewer` role, never
    19	executed; the compiler and linter carry the mechanical half of the
    20	same requirements. The mapping table compiles each Then into the
    21	judge-rubric assertion the reviewer scores. The scenarios project the
    22	[process-definition typedef](../artifacts/process-definition.md)'s
    23	requirements and the
    24	[process-definition guideline](../guidelines/process-definition.md)'s
    25	rules into a judge's rubric.
    26	
    27	## Scenarios
    28	
    29	Scenario 1: the definition is the single source its renderings claim
    30	  Given the process definition, its flow diagram, and its rendered
    31	  skill
    32	  When the diagram and skill are compared to the steps section
    33	  Then both correspond to the steps exactly — every step, prompt, and
    34	  branch present, nothing added — and both declare themselves
    35	  generated, never hand-edited
    36	
    37	Scenario 2: every outcome has a live witness
    38	  Given the outcomes list and the steps section
    39	  When each outcome's named witness is looked up
    40	  Then every outcome names a step, check, or branch that exists, and a
    41	  reader can say from the witness alone whether the outcome held for a
    42	  run
    43	
    44	Scenario 3: every loop declares its exits
    45	  Given every cycle in the flow
    46	  When its branch rows are read
    47	  Then each cycle carries a labeled reached-state success exit, a
    48	  round or budget cap, or both — no loop can run unbounded
    49	
    50	Scenario 4: steps read only what they list
    51	  Given each step's prompt, checks, and run template
    52	  When every reference in them is resolved
    53	  Then each resolves to a declared input or output of that step, and
    54	  no prompt directs the agent to load undeclared context
    55	
    56	Scenario 5: the run returns the artifact
    57	  Given the result declaration and the purpose
    58	  When they are compared
    59	  Then the run returns the artifact it exists to produce, or result is
    60	  absent and the outcomes pin the run's value
    61	
    62	Scenario 6: prose sits where prose belongs
    63	  Given every step record and the guiding statement
    64	  When each is read
    65	  Then step prose appears only in prompt fields, and the guiding
    66	  statement (when present) states a cross-step judgment, never a
    67	  sequence
    68	
    69	## Compile mapping (each Then/And → one judge-rubric assertion)
    70	
    71	| Scenario Then | Judge-rubric assertion |
    72	|---|---|
    73	| 1 — renderings correspond | "Walk the diagram and skill against the steps: name any step, prompt, or branch missing or added, and any rendering not marked generated. Empty list = pass." |
    74	| 2 — outcomes witnessed | "For each outcome, name the witnessing step/check/branch and confirm it exists. Any outcome with a missing or unverifiable witness = fail, cite it." |
    75	| 3 — loop exits declared | "List every cycle and its labeled exits. Any cycle without a success exit or cap = fail, cite it." |
    76	| 4 — declared reads only | "For each step, quote any reference in prompt/checks/run that is not a declared input or output, and any prompt directing undeclared context loads. Empty list = pass." |
    77	| 5 — artifact result | "Name the result value and what the purpose says the run produces. Mismatch, or a status-shaped result = fail; absent result justified by value-pinning outcomes = pass." |
    78	| 6 — prose placement | "Quote any prose in a step outside prompt, and quote the guiding statement if it sequences steps. Empty list = pass." |
    79	
    80	## Sources
    81	
    82	Gherkin syntax (readable G/W/T frame — syntax only, no runner);
    83	G-Eval–style rubric decomposition for the mapping table; the tests
    84	project the process-definition typedef's checklist and Commitment and
    85	the guideline's rules, per the definition-chain shape the
    86	principle-set chain established.

    92	| 1 | 2026-08-23 | update | Authored as the process-definition meta-chain's fitness set. |

    26	
    27	## Required frontmatter
    28	
    29	`type: process-definition`, `id`, `owner`, `status`, `created`,
    30	`updated`; `produces` (artifact
    31	types a run creates; the generic root `definition` covers runs creating
    32	definition documents; empty when the run's value is state change);
    33	`condition-language: cel`; optional: `carried-by` (the rendered skill's
    34	id), `condition-functions` (declared extensions, name and signature),
    35	`annotations` (process-level rendering metadata, keyed by rendering
    36	target); `hold-after` (ISO 8601 duration — the inactivity window after
    37	which the runtime holds a run; required for any process that carries a
    38	conversation); `ask-cap` (ISO 8601 duration — how long an ask may stand
    39	unanswered before its default applies; required for any process whose
    40	steps carry `asks`).
    41	
    42	## Required sections
    43	
    44	1. **Purpose** — one short paragraph.
    45	2. **Guiding statement** (optional) — directs judgment across the whole
    46	   process; the compiler copies it into every rendering.
    47	3. **Outcomes** — each names the step or check that witnesses it.
    48	4. **Roles** — roles and their accountability; role files carry identity,
    49	   never sequencing.
    50	5. **Flow (compiled)** — the diagram generated from the steps; never
    51	   edited by hand.
    52	6. **Data** — process-local value names. Simple types (JSON Schema
    53	   primitives) inline; every structured shape is a `$ref` to a defined
    54	   type with an explicit source: `from:` is a relative link to the
    55	   defining file, or `pkg:<package>/<type>` when the type lives in
    56	   another package and is fetched through that package's contract tool
    57	   (e.g. `shop-knowledge schema session-record`). Every distinct `$ref`
    58	   carries `from:` at least once; the linter verifies local sources
    59	   define the referenced type. No structured shape is ever defined here.
    60	   A value may declare `initial` — its value at run start.
    61	7. **Steps** — the executable part (shape below).
    62	8. **Derived checks** — a table: outcome, check, kind, where; every row
    63	   cites its clause or is deleted.
    64	
    65	Header elements 1–4 are bolded labels before the first heading; 5–8 are
    66	markdown headings in order (a section is a heading, per the
    67	artifact-typedef rule).
    68	
    69	## The steps section
    70	
    71	Top-level keys: `start` (first step id); optional `parameters` (data
    72	values supplied at instantiation rather than produced by any step);
    73	optional `result` (the data value a run returns — the artifact, not a
    74	status record; omit only when the outcomes pin the run's value). `end`
    75	is the reserved terminator id for `next`. Each step:
    76	
    77	- `id`, `name`; `run-by` — `{role, execution: agent}`,
    78	  `{role, execution: human}` (a role a person holds, e.g. an authority review), or `{execution: runtime}`; `fresh-context: true` where a role
    79	  must not carry memory between runs.
    80	- `inputs` / `outputs` — lists of declared data names; the typed contract
    81	  is the isolation mechanism (a step reads only what it lists).
    82	- Agent and human steps carry `prompt` — **the only prose allowed in a
    83	  step** (for a human step it is the question the review puts).
    84	- Runtime steps carry `set` (CEL assignments to data values or their
    85	  fields), `run` (command templates
    86	  with `${...}` interpolation from typed inputs — a scalar interpolates
    87	  as its value, an array as one shell word per element, a field of an
    88	  array's items as `${name[].field}` yielding one word per item in
    89	  item order, so a template may run a shell `for` over it or pair two
    90	  such fields positionally; `name` may be a data name or a field path
    91	  into one. A `run` step yields at most one output: the template's
    92	  standard output — split by line for an array value; `atomic: true`
    93	  binds the lines into one all-or-nothing act), or `branches`.
    94	- `checks` — CEL expressions over declared data.
    95	- Routing: `next`, or `branches` of `{label, when (CEL), next}` rows plus
    96	  one `else`. **Every loop declares its exits as labeled branch rows** —
    97	  a reached-state success exit, a round or budget cap, or both.
    98	- `asks` — optional list of role ids the step may put an ask to (the
    99	  [`ask`](../types/ask.md) data type). An agent or human step listed
   100	  with `asks` may return an ask in place of its outputs; a step without
   101	  `asks` may not ask. A process with asking steps declares an `ask` data
   102	  value (`$ref: ask`) and lists it in each asking step's inputs. Every
   103	  ask names a `default` and a `checkpoint`; the step's prompt states
   104	  what kind of information it may ask for — never a judgment the step's
   105	  role owes. A step returns at most one ask per run — the loop's exit —
   106	  and a second resolves `defaulted` at once. Early steps ask cheaply;
   107	  an ask from a late step wastes the work not in its checkpoint.
   108	- `annotations` — per-step rendering metadata keyed by target (e.g.
   109	  `fabro: {model, max_attempts}`); the definition itself ignores them.
   110	- `run-by: {execution: sub-process, process: <process-id>, from: <source>}`
   111	  runs another process definition as one step: the step's inputs map to
   112	  the child's parameters and its outputs receive the child's result. A
   113	  conversation invoked this way is a branched conversation: the child's
   114	  anchor records the parent run.
   115	
   116	## Run lifecycle
   117	
   118	A run is one execution of a process, anchored to a work item in the
   119	registry. Run states: `running`, `held`, `done`, `cancelled`.
   120	
   121	- **Hold** pauses a run: the current step and every data value persist in
   122	  the run's anchor, and the work item records the state. A held run is
   123	  resumed at its recorded step or cancelled with a reason — never
   124	  silently dropped.
   125	- The `hold-after` window makes parking automatic: a run with no activity
   126	  inside the window is held by the runtime. Unfinished work parks itself
   127	  with a named resume point; nothing dangles in the lead repo.
   128	- **Ask** holds a run the same way, with the ask recorded on the anchor
   129	  and routed to whoever fills the role it names — a person or an agent;
   130	  the answer is written to the ask and the run resumes at the asking
   131	  step with the ask in its inputs, in a fresh context loaded from the
   132	  step's declared inputs and the checkpoint. There is no synchronous
   133	  form: no step waits in place for an answer. An unanswered ask resolves
   134	  to its `default` at the process's `ask-cap` (an ISO 8601 duration,
   135	  required for any process whose steps carry `asks`), and the run
   136	  resumes on the default with the ask marked `defaulted`; cancelling a
   137	  held run marks its ask `cancelled`. Answering is an activity of the
   138	  answering role: a human step for a human-held role, or a step the
   139	  answering role's process names — those steps are defined in the
   140	  processes that answer, not here. The registry that anchors runs
   141	  records every ask; asks per run, per role, and per kind are read from
   142	  it. An ask that recurs across runs is a gap in a definition; the
   143	  answering role files the definition change, and the ask stops.
   144	- **Cancel** closes the run's work item with a reason and files the
   145	  resulting actions the outcomes demand.
   146	
   147	## Rendering contract
   148	
   149	The compiler generates: the in-document flow diagram (typed inputs and
   150	outputs on every node; the result on the end node) and the skill —
   151	front-matter (`generated: true`, `generated-by`, `derived-from`,
   152	`source`, `source-digest`) and body (purpose, guiding statement, result,
   153	diagram, one section per step with the prompt verbatim). Conformance
   154	check: re-run the compiler and diff.
   155	
   156	## Commitment (Definition of Done)
   157	
   158	A process definition is done when it compiles — every `$ref` resolves,
   159	the diagram and renderings generate, `result` (if declared) names a data
   160	value — and every loop declares its exit. **Consequence on failure:** it
   161	cannot be dispatched, carried by a skill, or cited by a check.
   162	
   163	## Sources
   164	
   165	ISO/IEC/IEEE 24774 (name/purpose/outcomes header); GitHub Actions (step
   166	records with typed inputs/outputs); CNCF Serverless Workflow
   167	(data-condition transitions); CEL — Common Expression Language
   168	(mechanically translatable conditions); Essence-style state exits plus a
   169	round cap (the dual-exit rule).
   170	
   171	## Derived review checklist
   172	
   173	- Compiles clean: refs resolve, diagram and renderings regenerate
   174	  byte-stable. *(Commitment)*
   175	- No prose inside step records outside `prompt` fields; section
   176	  introduction prose is body text, not step content. *(§The steps section)*
   177	- Every loop has labeled success and/or cap exits. *(§The steps section)*
   178	- Every step with `asks` belongs to a process with `ask-cap` and lists
   179	  the `ask` value in its inputs; every ask names a default and a
   180	  checkpoint, and its `to` is in the step's `asks`; one ask per step per
   181	  run. *(§The steps section, §Run lifecycle)*
   182	- Outcomes each name a witness. *(§Required sections 3)*
   183	- `result`, if absent, is justified by outcomes that pin the run's value.
   184	  *(§The steps section)*
   185	
   186	## Document History
   187	
   188	| Version | Date | Kind | Entry |
   189	|---|---|---|---|
   190	| 1 | 2026-08-19 | update | Authored (seed layer); earlier history, if any, in the repository history. |
   191	| 1 | 2026-08-22 | state | draft → approved. |
   192	| 2 | 2026-08-23 | update | Owner direction: decision-ledger references removed — changes stand on their own; history entries and text no longer cite numbered decisions. |
   193	| 3 | 2026-08-25 | update | Owner direction: a near-synonym of "role" retired and banned. |
   194	| 4 | 2026-08-25 | update | Owner decision: the ask mechanism defined, held-and-resumed only — a step may carry `asks` (role ids) and return an `ask` data value in place of its outputs; the run holds, the role answers, the step resumes in a fresh context from its inputs and the ask's checkpoint; `ask-cap` bounds an unanswered ask with its default; a recurring ask is a definition gap. No synchronous form. |
   195	| 4 | 2026-08-25 | review | Screened with the ask data type: findings — the ask loop lacked an exit; the resumed ask had no data name; answering had no named activity; the recurrence measure had no channel; an old use of "ask" collided. Repaired in place: one ask per step per run, the `ask` value declared and listed, answering placed in the answering role's process, the registry named as the count's home, wording fixed. |
   196	| 5 | 2026-08-28 | update | Owner direction, from the scenario-assignment screen: how arrays and item fields interpolate into a `run` template defined, so a fan-out over contexts is a defined form. |

    11	---
    12	
    13	# Guideline: process definition
    14	
    15	**Voice principle.** Write for the runtime that must construct a
    16	workflow from the steps and the reviewer who must connect every
    17	outcome to its witness: every element either executes, routes,
    18	witnesses, or declares a contract — explanation lives in body prose,
    19	never inside a step.
    20	
    21	**Highlights (the layer compiled into generating context):** every
    22	outcome names its witness · prose inside a step only in `prompt` ·
    23	every loop declares a labeled success exit, a cap, or both · a step
    24	reads only what it lists — the declared list is the context load list ·
    25	the result is the artifact, not a status.
    26	
    27	**Layers:** this guideline adds process-definition rules on top of the
    28	[base writing style](base-writing-style.md); the base always applies
    29	and is never overridden. When rules conflict, an approved principle
    30	beats the
    31	[process-definition typedef](../artifacts/process-definition.md),
    32	which beats this guideline.
    33	
    34	---
    35	
    36	## Rules
    37	
    38	**1. Give every outcome a witness.**
    39	Before: "O1. The review is high-quality."
    40	After: "O1. Every decision is applied before the next exchange —
    41	witnessed by the check on `apply`."
    42	*Test:* read each outcome. *Criterion:* it names the step, check, or
    43	branch that witnesses it, and that witness exists in the steps
    44	section. *Decision:* yes/no per outcome.
    45	*Derived check:* judged — scenario 2 of
    46	[process-definition.fitness.md](../fitness/process-definition.fitness.md).
    47	
    48	**2. Keep prose out of steps.**
    49	Before: a step record carrying "This step is important because
    50	reviewers often forget to check the register."
    51	After: the sentence moved to body text before the steps section, or
    52	into the step's `prompt` if the agent needs it.
    53	*Test:* scan every step record. *Criterion:* prose appears only in
    54	`prompt` fields; runtime steps carry `set`, `run`, or `branches` and
    55	no sentences. *Decision:* yes/no per step.
    56	*Derived check:* mechanical — the no-prose row of the typedef's
    57	derived review checklist.
    58	
    59	**3. Declare every loop's exits, labeled.**
    60	Before: revise → review → revise with no cap and an unlabeled edge.
    61	After: "failsafe exit: round >= 3 → park" and "success exit: clean →
    62	approve" as labeled branch rows.
    63	*Test:* trace every cycle in the flow. *Criterion:* each cycle carries
    64	a labeled reached-state success exit, a round or budget cap, or both.
    65	*Decision:* yes/no per cycle.
    66	*Derived check:* judged — fitness scenario 3; mechanical presence in
    67	the loop-exit row of the typedef checklist.
    68	
    69	**4. Let a step read only what it lists.**
    70	Before: a prompt telling the agent to "check the register and any
    71	related records you find useful."
    72	After: the register declared as an input; the prompt references only
    73	declared inputs.
    74	*Test:* compare each step's prompt, checks, and run template to its
    75	declared inputs and outputs. *Criterion:* every reference resolves to
    76	a declared name; the declared list is the step's context load list —
    77	an undeclared load is a defect. *Decision:* yes/no per step.
    78	*Derived check:* judged — fitness scenario 4.
    79	
    80	**5. Return the artifact, not a status.**
    81	Before: "result: report — a summary of what the run did."
    82	After: "result: set — the principle-set the run produced."
    83	*Test:* read the `result` declaration against the purpose. *Criterion:*
    84	the run returns the artifact it exists to produce, or omits `result`
    85	with outcomes that pin the run's value. *Decision:* yes/no per
    86	process.
    87	*Derived check:* judged — fitness scenario 5.
    88	
    89	**6. Direct judgment with the guiding statement, not instructions.**
    90	Before: "Guiding statement: first draft, then review, then ship."
    91	After: "Guiding statement: everything binding lands in the governed
    92	artifacts it changes; nothing binding lives only in the transcript."
    93	*Test:* read the guiding statement. *Criterion:* it states a judgment
    94	that applies across every step, never a sequence — sequences are
    95	steps. *Decision:* yes/no per statement (vacuously pass when absent).
    96	*Derived check:* judged — fitness scenario 6.
    97	
    98	## Sources
    99	
   100	Style-guide anatomy per the quality-guideline typedef; Deming's
   101	operational definitions (test, criterion, decision per rule); the
   102	external forms the process-definition typedef adopts (ISO/IEC/IEEE
   103	24774 header, GitHub-Actions-shaped steps, CEL conditions, dual-exit
   104	loops) — this guideline projects them into authoring rules; the before
   105	examples are generic counter-examples, never drawn from this product's
   106	history.

    41	  reader can say from the witness alone whether the outcome held for a

    18	A backlog order is the PO role's ordered list of requirements within
    19	the PM role's framing — the PO role's exclusive decision — as submitted for
    20	the PM role's check. These scenarios are the criteria set the
    21	[PO output check](../processes/po-output-check.md) screens an order
    22	against, alongside the framing (criterion `framing`). Evaluated by the
    23	`cold-reviewer` role, never executed. The judge's model and prompt
    24	version are recorded with each round verdict.
    25	The judge reads only the criteria set, the framing, and the artifact;
    26	every scenario therefore asks for what the artifact itself carries, and
    27	a fact it must carry — a term's definition, a reference, a reason — is
    28	what these scenarios make it carry. The check runs
    29	within the [backlog-ordering](../processes/backlog-ordering.md)
    30	process; the
    31	[backlog-order typedef](../artifacts/backlog-order.md) carries the
    32	form these scenarios judge. Scenario 1 overlaps the
    33	process's `framing` criterion by design: the process passes one
    34	framing and an order spans many. What the
    35	judge cannot catch from the order alone — a recommendation omitted, a
    36	wrong context — is the solutions architect role's to raise through its
    37	interface with the PO role.
    38	
    39	## Scenarios
    40	
    41	Scenario 1: every item serves a framing
    42	  Given each item in the order
    43	  When its framing reference is read
    44	  Then it names the framing it serves, or is marked declined with a
    45	  reason
    46	
    47	Scenario 2: the order states the priority it follows
    48	  Given the order's statement of the roadmap priority it was made
    49	  against
    50	  When the order is compared with that statement
    51	  Then items serving a higher-priority framing precede items serving a
    52	  lower one, or the order states a reason for each exception
    53	
    54	Scenario 3: enabler work is placed or declined with reasons
    55	  Given the order's list of enabler recommendations received from the
    56	  solutions architect role
    57	  When the order is read
    58	  Then each recommendation appears in the order with its position
    59	  reasoned, or is declined with a reason
    60	
    61	Scenario 4: the order names each item's context
    62	  Given each item
    63	  When it is read
    64	  Then it names the Bounded Context that owns it, and an item crossing
    65	  contexts is marked as such with the escalation to the PM role named
    66	
    67	Scenario 5: the next item says whether it is ready
    68	  Given the first item not yet taken up
    69	  When it is read
    70	  Then the order marks it ready and links the feature it states is
    71	  checked (passed the PO output check), or marks it not ready and names
    72	  what it waits on
    73	
    74	## Compile mapping (each Then → one judge-rubric assertion)
    75	
    76	| Scenario Then | Judge-rubric assertion |
    77	|---|---|
    78	| 1 — serves a framing | "For each item: framing named, or declined with a reason? Cite any item with neither." |
    79	| 2 — follows stated priority | "Compare the order with the priority it states; cite each inversion and whether a reason is stated. Any unreasoned inversion = fail." |

    81	| 4 — context named | "Does each item name its owning Bounded Context, with cross-context items marked and their escalation named? Cite any that does not." |
    82	| 5 — next item ready | "Is the first untaken item marked ready with the artifact it states is checked linked, or not ready with what it waits on? Cite." |

    12	# Guideline: backlog order
    13	
    14	**Voice principle.** Write the order for the shop deciding what to
    15	take up next and the PM checking that the order follows the priority:
    16	every item says which framing it serves, which context owns it, and
    17	why it sits where it sits.
    18	
    19	**Highlights (the layer compiled into generating context):** the
    20	priority followed, stated in the document · every exception reasoned ·
    21	every enabler recommendation placed or declined with a reason · every
    22	item's framing and context named; cross-context items marked with
    23	their escalation · the next item's readiness stated.
    24	
    25	**Layers:** this guideline adds backlog-order rules on top of the
    26	[base writing style](base-writing-style.md); the base always applies
    27	and is never overridden. When rules conflict, an approved principle
    28	beats the [backlog-order typedef](../artifacts/backlog-order.md), which
    29	beats this guideline. Every rule feeds the
    30	[backlog-order fitness set](../fitness/backlog-order.fitness.md),
    31	scored in the [PO output check](../processes/po-output-check.md).
    32	
    33	---
    34	
    35	## Rules
    36	
    37	**1. State the priority you followed, and reason every exception.**
    38	Before: an ordered list with no reference to any priority.
    39	After: "Priority followed: the PM's roadmap priority of 2026-08-20
    40	(linked): failure visibility, then alerting, then archive. Exception:
    41	item 3 (archive retention) precedes alerting because the archive
    42	feature blocks the retention bug the shop reported."
    43	*Test:* read the priority-followed section (§1) and compare the order
    44	against the priority it states.
    45	*Criterion:* the priority is stated; every inversion carries a reason.
    46	*Decision:* yes/no per order.
    47	*Derived check:* judged — backlog-order fitness scenario 2.
    48	
    49	**2. Every item names its framing or is declined with a reason.**
    50	Before: "Item 4: refactor status handling."
    51	After: "Item 4: status vocabulary alignment — serves the
    52	failure-visibility framing (linked)." or "Declined: a status
    53	refactor with no framed outcome; returned to the architect as enabler
    54	work."
    55	*Test:* read each item's framing reference. *Criterion:* a framing is
    56	named, or the item is marked declined with its reason. *Decision:*
    57	yes/no per item.
    58	*Derived check:* judged — backlog-order fitness scenario 1.
    59	
    60	**3. Place or decline each enabler recommendation, with reasons.**
    61	Before: an architect's recommendation absent from the order.
    62	After: "Enabler recommendations received: (a) list contract version 2
    63	— placed at item 2, since item 3 depends on it; (b) status
    64	consolidation — declined this order, no framing served yet."
    65	*Test:* read the enabler-recommendations section (§2) against the
    66	recommendations the order lists as received. *Criterion:* each is placed with a reasoned position or
    67	declined with a reason. *Decision:* yes/no per recommendation.
    68	*Derived check:* judged — backlog-order fitness scenario 3.
    69	
    70	**4. Name the owning context; mark and escalate cross-context items.**
    71	Before: "Item 5: export failed runs as CSV."
    72	After: "Item 5: export failed runs as CSV — reporting and export
    73	contexts; cross-context, escalated to the PM role (linked)."
    74	*Test:* read each item's context. *Criterion:* the owning Bounded
    75	Context is named; an item crossing contexts is marked and its
    76	escalation named. *Decision:* yes/no per item.
    77	*Derived check:* judged — backlog-order fitness scenario 4.

    79	**5. Say whether the next item is ready.**

    82	or "Next: item 1 — not ready; waits on the designer's usability

    15	
    16	# Lead PO
    17	
    18	You hold the role that makes the requirements. From the
    19	[PM role](lead-pm.md)'s *framing* — its recorded statement of the problem a request is about
    20	and the outcome it serves (see the [glossary](../glossary.md)) — you
    21	author the artifacts that say what the product is supposed to do:
    22	[features](../artifacts/feature.md) — a Gherkin Feature with its
    23	acceptance scenarios, made from an [initiative](../artifacts/initiative.md),
    24	authored by this role alone — [product decision records](../artifacts/product-decision-record.md),
    25	and the [backlog order](../artifacts/backlog-order.md). Shops receive
    26	the scenarios assigned to them, never a document of their own. You order
    27	the backlog, in the
    28	[backlog-ordering](../processes/backlog-ordering.md) process. Scope and vocabulary questions from any Bounded Context
    29	shop resolve against your artifacts. The PM role checks what you make
    30	against the framing; you make, you do not check your own work.
    31	
    32	**Standard of judgment:** you own the commitment, you do not take
    33	orders — you decline scope that serves no framed outcome and record
    34	the reason. You say what, never how. You author alone; the PO output check
    35	is the check your text meets; the repository sweep at assignment and
    36	the shops' clarifies after dispatch catch what authoring cannot see;
    37	the designer's and architect's criteria ride on your scenarios.
    38	
    39	**Accountable for:**
    40	- Requirements artifacts the rest of the shop can act on — features,
    41	  product decision records, the backlog order — each traceable to the
    42	  framing it serves.
    43	- Features written in Gherkin: a narrative saying who and why, and
    44	  scenarios each tagged, identified by a hash of its text so that a
    45	  changed scenario is a new scenario, and testable against the running
    46	  system — a feature's scenarios may be owned by several shops, each
    47	  named for assignment. Authored in the
    48	  [feature-authoring](../processes/feature-authoring.md) process.
    49	- The backlog: its content and order within the framing, structured
    50	  to mirror the [solutions architect](lead-solutions-architect.md)'s
    51	  decomposition.
    52	- Scope and vocabulary answers to clarify questions from Bounded
    53	  Context shops, grounded in the requirements artifacts.
    54	- The requirements picture readable from the artifacts alone, without
    55	  asking their author; new domain vocabulary added to the glossary.
    56	
    57	**Domain (exclusive):** backlog order — this role alone decides which
    58	requirement the shops take up next, within the framing.
    59	
    60	**Decision rights.**
    61	- *Decides:* backlog order (exclusive). The content of the artifacts
    62	  it submits is this role's authorship and the PM role's check; which
    63	  scenario a clarify resolves against is this role's answer, open to
    64	  the shop's evidence.
    65	- *Recommends:* scope changes to the PM role, with reasons; nothing
    66	  on which context owns a scenario — that is the solutions architect's assignment.
    67	- *Places or declines in the backlog, with reasons:* enabler work the
    68	  solutions architect recommends — an exercise of the exclusive
    69	  domain, not a recommendation.
    70	- *Escalates to the PM role:* scope conflicts; a scenario the
    71	  solutions architect reports as infeasible; a returned
    72	  crossing-contexts scenario no split within the framing can resolve —
    73	  the split itself is this role's own act; a framing the artifacts
    74	  cannot be written from.
    75	- *Never decides:* whether a problem is worth solving (the PM's); the
    76	  pass or fail of its own output (the PM's check); how a behavior is
    77	  built (the shops' and the architect's); which context owns a
    78	  behavior (the architect's).
    79	
    80	**Admissible evidence:** the PM role's recorded framing; the feature
    81	repository read in full — the lead shop's feature artifacts,
    82	authoritative for what is specified; the solutions architect's
    83	decomposition, for where a scenario lands, and its non-functional
    84	constraints; the designer's criteria. Not authoritative: a
    85	stakeholder document transcribed into tickets; a scenario that has
    86	not passed the PO output check; this role's own memory of what the
    87	PM meant.
    88	
    89	**Interfaces:**
    90	- The PM role: framed intent in; requirements artifacts, backlog
    91	  order, and scope questions out, for the check.
    92	- The solutions architect role: PM-checked features out, for
    93	  assignment of each scenario to the Bounded Context that owns it; enabler recommendations, non-functional constraints, and
    94	  decomposition changes in.
    95	- Bounded Context shops: their scenarios reach them through
    96	  assignment; clarify questions on scope and vocabulary in, answers
    97	  out; a conflict with behavior already
    98	  specified is caught by the repository sweep at assignment or comes
    99	  back as a return, never asked about during authoring.
   100	- Asks out, to the PM role: a question the framing cannot answer,
   101	  sent with a proposed default.
   102	
   103	**Knowledge and skills:** requirements authoring; Gherkin as an
   104	acceptance language; backlog ordering by outcome; the product's domain
   105	language; the [working principle set](../principles.md).
   106	
   107	**Anti-rationalization:**
   108	- "The stakeholder's list is the requirement." → A list is input; the
   109	  framing decides what serves an outcome.
   110	- "No shop will object, skip the sweep." → The repository sweep at
   111	  assignment is the check on specified behavior; authoring does not
   112	  skip it by assertion.
   113	- "It's obviously done." → Done is the PM role's check against the
   114	  framing, not this role's opinion of its own output.
   115	- "The architect said it can't be built, so drop it." → Infeasible
   116	  escalates to the PM role for re-framing; it is not a scope decision
   117	  here.
   118	- "I'll specify how, it's faster." → The how is the shops'; specifying
   119	  it removes their ownership and the architect's check.

    20	the PM role's check. These scenarios are the criteria set the
    21	[PO output check](../processes/po-output-check.md) screens an order
    22	against, alongside the framing (criterion `framing`). Evaluated by the
    23	`cold-reviewer` role, never executed. The judge's model and prompt
    24	version are recorded with each round verdict.
    25	The judge reads only the criteria set, the framing, and the artifact;
    26	every scenario therefore asks for what the artifact itself carries, and
    27	a fact it must carry — a term's definition, a reference, a reason — is
    28	what these scenarios make it carry. The check runs
    29	within the [backlog-ordering](../processes/backlog-ordering.md)
    30	process; the
    31	[backlog-order typedef](../artifacts/backlog-order.md) carries the
    32	form these scenarios judge. Scenario 1 overlaps the
    33	process's `framing` criterion by design: the process passes one
    34	framing and an order spans many. What the
    35	judge cannot catch from the order alone — a recommendation omitted, a
    36	wrong context — is the solutions architect role's to raise through its
    37	interface with the PO role.
    38	
    39	## Scenarios
    40	
    41	Scenario 1: every item serves a framing
    42	  Given each item in the order
    43	  When its framing reference is read
    44	  Then it names the framing it serves, or is marked declined with a
    45	  reason
    46	
    47	Scenario 2: the order states the priority it follows
    48	  Given the order's statement of the roadmap priority it was made
    49	  against
    50	  When the order is compared with that statement
    51	  Then items serving a higher-priority framing precede items serving a
    52	  lower one, or the order states a reason for each exception
    53	
    54	Scenario 3: enabler work is placed or declined with reasons
    55	  Given the order's list of enabler recommendations received from the
    56	  solutions architect role
    57	  When the order is read
    58	  Then each recommendation appears in the order with its position
    59	  reasoned, or is declined with a reason
    60	
    61	Scenario 4: the order names each item's context
    62	  Given each item
    63	  When it is read
    64	  Then it names the Bounded Context that owns it, and an item crossing
    65	  contexts is marked as such with the escalation to the PM role named
    66	
    67	Scenario 5: the next item says whether it is ready
    68	  Given the first item not yet taken up
    69	  When it is read
    70	  Then the order marks it ready and links the feature it states is
    71	  checked (passed the PO output check), or marks it not ready and names
    72	  what it waits on
    73	
    74	## Compile mapping (each Then → one judge-rubric assertion)
    75	
    76	| Scenario Then | Judge-rubric assertion |
    77	|---|---|
    78	| 1 — serves a framing | "For each item: framing named, or declined with a reason? Cite any item with neither." |
    79	| 2 — follows stated priority | "Compare the order with the priority it states; cite each inversion and whether a reason is stated. Any unreasoned inversion = fail." |
    80	| 3 — enablers placed or declined | "For each recommendation the order lists: placed with a reasoned position, or declined with a reason? Cite any that is neither." |
    81	| 4 — context named | "Does each item name its owning Bounded Context, with cross-context items marked and their escalation named? Cite any that does not." |
    82	| 5 — next item ready | "Is the first untaken item marked ready with the artifact it states is checked linked, or not ready with what it waits on? Cite." |
    83

    94	| 3 | 2026-08-26 | state | draft → approved by the owner. |

     2	type: quality-guideline
     3	id: backlog-order-guideline
     4	target-type: backlog-order
     5	owner: product-authority
     6	status: draft
     7	version: 3
     8	created: 2026-08-27
     9	updated: 2026-08-28
    10	---
    11	
    12	# Guideline: backlog order
    13	
    14	**Voice principle.** Write the order for the shop deciding what to
    15	take up next and the PM checking that the order follows the priority:
    16	every item says which framing it serves, which context owns it, and
    17	why it sits where it sits.
    18	
    19	**Highlights (the layer compiled into generating context):** the
    20	priority followed, stated in the document · every exception reasoned ·
    21	every enabler recommendation placed or declined with a reason · every
    22	item's framing and context named; cross-context items marked with
    23	their escalation · the next item's readiness stated.
    24	
    25	**Layers:** this guideline adds backlog-order rules on top of the
    26	[base writing style](base-writing-style.md); the base always applies
    27	and is never overridden. When rules conflict, an approved principle
    28	beats the [backlog-order typedef](../artifacts/backlog-order.md), which
    29	beats this guideline. Every rule feeds the
    30	[backlog-order fitness set](../fitness/backlog-order.fitness.md),
    31	scored in the [PO output check](../processes/po-output-check.md).
    32	
    33	---
    34	
    35	## Rules
    36	
    37	**1. State the priority you followed, and reason every exception.**
    38	Before: an ordered list with no reference to any priority.
    39	After: "Priority followed: the PM's roadmap priority of 2026-08-20
    40	(linked): failure visibility, then alerting, then archive. Exception:
    41	item 3 (archive retention) precedes alerting because the archive
    42	feature blocks the retention bug the shop reported."
    43	*Test:* read the priority-followed section (§1) and compare the order
    44	against the priority it states.
    45	*Criterion:* the priority is stated; every inversion carries a reason.
    46	*Decision:* yes/no per order.
    47	*Derived check:* judged — backlog-order fitness scenario 2.
    48	
    49	**2. Every item names its framing or is declined with a reason.**
    50	Before: "Item 4: refactor status handling."
    51	After: "Item 4: status vocabulary alignment — serves the
    52	failure-visibility framing (linked)." or "Declined: a status
    53	refactor with no framed outcome; returned to the architect as enabler
    54	work."
    55	*Test:* read each item's framing reference. *Criterion:* a framing is
    56	named, or the item is marked declined with its reason. *Decision:*
    57	yes/no per item.
    58	*Derived check:* judged — backlog-order fitness scenario 1.
    59	
    60	**3. Place or decline each enabler recommendation, with reasons.**
    61	Before: an architect's recommendation absent from the order.
    62	After: "Enabler recommendations received: (a) list contract version 2
    63	— placed at item 2, since item 3 depends on it; (b) status
    64	consolidation — declined this order, no framing served yet."
    65	*Test:* read the enabler-recommendations section (§2) against the
    66	recommendations the order lists as received. *Criterion:* each is placed with a reasoned position or
    67	declined with a reason. *Decision:* yes/no per recommendation.
    68	*Derived check:* judged — backlog-order fitness scenario 3.
    69	
    70	**4. Name the owning context; mark and escalate cross-context items.**
    71	Before: "Item 5: export failed runs as CSV."
    72	After: "Item 5: export failed runs as CSV — reporting and export
    73	contexts; cross-context, escalated to the PM role (linked)."
    74	*Test:* read each item's context. *Criterion:* the owning Bounded
    75	Context is named; an item crossing contexts is marked and its
    76	escalation named. *Decision:* yes/no per item.
    77	*Derived check:* judged — backlog-order fitness scenario 4.
    78	
    79	**5. Say whether the next item is ready.**
    80	Before: the first untaken item with no readiness statement.
    81	After: "Next: item 1 — ready; its feature (linked) states it is checked."
    82	or "Next: item 1 — not ready; waits on the designer's usability
    83	criteria."
    84	*Test:* read the first untaken item. *Criterion:* it is marked ready
    85	with the artifact it states is checked linked, or not ready with what
    86	it waits on. *Decision:* yes/no per order.
    87	*Derived check:* judged — backlog-order fitness scenario 5.
    88

    92	|---|---|---|---|
    93	| 1 | 2026-08-27 | update | Authored by owner direction to complete the type's definition chain; each rule maps to one fitness scenario. |
